requirements.description: The undertaking shall report on sustainability matters based on the double materiality principle (impact materiality and financial materiality).

The undertaking shall perform a materiality assessment (impact and financial) as the starting point for ESRS reporting, to identify the material impacts, risks and opportunities to be reported. A sustainability matter is material when it meets the criteria for impact materiality or financial materiality, or both.

In conducting the materiality assessment, the undertaking shall consider stakeholders (affected stakeholders and users of sustainability statements). Engagement with affected stakeholders is central to due diligence and the sustainability materiality assessment, including identifying and assessing actual and potential negative impacts that inform identification of material impacts for reporting.

The undertaking shall apply double materiality (impact and financial). It shall consider interdependencies between impact and financial materiality, generally starting from impacts while also considering that some material risks/opportunities may not be related to impacts. It shall use appropriate qualitative and/or quantitative thresholds to determine which impacts, risks and opportunities are material and which sustainability matters are material for reporting purposes.

To determine impact materiality, the undertaking shall assess material actual or potential positive or negative impacts on people or the environment across its own operations and upstream/downstream value chain over short-, medium- and long-term. For negative impacts: materiality is based on severity (scale, scope, irremediable character) for actual impacts, and severity and likelihood for potential impacts (with severity taking precedence over likelihood for potential negative human rights impacts). For positive impacts: materiality is based on scale and scope (actual) and scale, scope and likelihood (potential).

To determine financial materiality, the undertaking shall identify sustainability matters that trigger or could reasonably be expected to trigger material financial effects on development, financial position, financial performance, cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital over short-, medium- or long-term. Financial materiality includes risks/opportunities beyond the scope of consolidation (e.g., from business relationships). Dependencies on natural, human and social resources shall be considered as potential sources of financial risks/opportunities. The materiality of risks and opportunities is assessed based on likelihood and magnitude of potential financial effects.

In identifying and assessing impacts, risks and opportunities, the undertaking shall focus on where they are likely to arise based on activities, business relationships, geographies or other factors, and extend the assessment/reporting boundary to include material impacts, risks and opportunities connected through direct and indirect upstream and downstream value chain relationships, consistent with due diligence and the double materiality assessment.

The outcome of the undertaking’s sustainability due diligence process informs the assessment of material impacts, risks and opportunities. Due diligence is an ongoing process to identify, prevent, mitigate and account for actual and potential negative impacts across own operations and value chain; prioritisation based on severity and likelihood informs the assessment of material impacts and supports identification of material sustainability risks and opportunities.

If actions to address certain impacts/risks or to benefit from opportunities in relation to one sustainability matter create material negative impacts or material risks in other sustainability matters, the undertaking shall disclose the existence of those material negative impacts/risks together with the actions that generate them (with cross-references) and describe how they are addressed under the relevant topic.

requirements.requirement_id: ESRS 1 §26 (link to ESRS 2 disclosures on process and outcomes)
requirements.description: The undertaking’s materiality assessment process and the resulting material impacts, risks and opportunities are to be disclosed via ESRS 2 (IRO-1 for the process; SBM-3 for the resulting material IROs).

summary: Under ESRS 1, the undertaking’s answer should explain that it performed a double materiality assessment (impact and financial), using appropriate qualitative/quantitative thresholds and considering interdependencies between the two dimensions. It should describe how stakeholders—especially affected stakeholders—were engaged and how due diligence outcomes informed identification and prioritisation of actual and potential impacts across own operations and the upstream/downstream value chain. It should explain the criteria used: impact materiality based on severity (scale, scope, irremediable character) and likelihood (for potential impacts), and financial materiality based on likelihood and magnitude of potential material financial effects (including from dependencies on natural, human and social resources and from business relationships beyond consolidation). Finally, it should present which sustainability matters were identified as material from both perspectives (i.e., meeting impact and financial materiality criteria), noting any cross-matter trade-offs where actions on one matter create material impacts/risks on another.

Standard: ESRS 1
Title: GENERAL REQUIREMENTS
[objective.1] Categories of ESRS Standards, reporting areas and drafting conventions
[objective.2] Specifically, ESRS specify the information that an undertaking shall disclose about its material impacts, risks and opportunities in relation to environmental, social, and governance sustainability matters. ESRS do not require undertakings to disclose any information on environmental, social and governance topics covered by ESRS when the undertaking has assessed the topic in question as non-material (See Appendix E of this Standard “Flowchart for determining disclosures to be included”).The information disclosed in accordance with ESRS enables users of the sustainability statement to understand the undertaking’s material impacts on people and environment and the material effects of sustainability matters on the undertaking’s development, performance and position.
[objective.3] The objective of this Standard (ESRS 1) is to provide an understanding of the architecture of ESRS, the drafting conventions and fundamental concepts used, and the general requirements for preparing and presenting sustainability information in accordance with Directive 2013/34/EU, as amended by Directive (EU) 2022/2464.
[content[0].title] 1.1 Categories of ESRS standards
[content[0].paragraphs[0].4] There are three categories of ESRS: (a) cross-cutting standards; (b) topical standards (Environmental, Social and Governance standards); and (c) sector-specific standards. Cross-cutting standards and topical standards are sector-agnostic, meaning that they apply to all undertakings regardless of which sector or sectors the undertaking operates in.
[content[0].paragraphs[1].5] The cross-cutting standards ESRS 1 General requirements and ESRS 2 General disclosures apply to the sustainability matters covered by topical standards and sector-specific standards.
[content[0].paragraphs[2].6] This standard (ESRS 1) describes the architecture of ESRS standards, explains drafting conventions and fundamental concepts, and sets out general requirements for preparing and presenting sustainability-related information.
[content[0].paragraphs[3].7] ESRS 2 establishes Disclosure Requirements on the information that the undertaking shall provide at a general level across all material sustainability matters on the reporting areas governance, strategy, impact, risk and opportunity management, and metrics and targets.
[content[0].paragraphs[4].8] Topical ESRS cover a sustainability topic and are structured into topics and sub-topics, and where necessary sub-sub- topics. The table in Application Requirement 16 (AR 16) to this standard provides an overview of the sustainability topics, sub-topics and sub-sub-topics (collectively ‘sustainability matters’) covered by topical ESRS. (1) Directive 2013/34/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 26 June 2013 on the annual financial statements, consolidated financial statements and related reports of certain types of undertakings, amending Directive 2006/43/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directives 78/660/EEC and 83/349/EEC (OJ L 182, 29.6.2013, p. 19). (2) Directive (EU) 2022/2464 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 December 2022 amending Regulation (EU) No 537/2014, Directive 2004/109/EC, Directive 2006/43/EC and Directive 2013/34/EU, as regards corporate sustainability reporting (OJ L 322, 16.12.2022, p. 15).
[content[0].paragraphs[5].9] Topical ESRS can include specific requirements that complement the general level Disclosure Requirements of ESRS
[content[0].paragraphs[6].2] ESRS 2 Appendix C Disclosure/Application Requirements in topical ESRS that are applicable jointly with ESRS 2 General Disclosures provides a list of the additional requirements in topical ESRS that the undertaking shall apply in conjunction with the general level disclosure requirements of ESRS 2.
[content[0].paragraphs[7].10] Sector-specific standards are applicable to all undertakings within a sector. They address impacts, risks and opportunities that are likely to be material for all undertakings in a specific sector and that are not covered, or not sufficiently covered, by topical standards. Sector-specific standards are multi-topical and cover the topics that are most relevant to the sector in question. Sector-specific standards achieve a high degree of comparability.
[content[0].paragraphs[8].11] In addition to the disclosure requirements laid down in the three categories of ESRS, when an undertaking concludes that an impact, risk or opportunity is not covered or not covered with sufficient granularity by an ESRS but is material due to its specific facts and circumstances, it shall provide additional entity-specific disclosures to enable users to understand the undertaking’s sustainability-related impacts, risks or opportunities. Application requirements AR 1 to AR 5 provide further guidance regarding entity-specific disclosures.
[content[1].title] 1.2 Reporting areas and minimum content disclosure requirements on policies, actions, targets and metrics
[content[1].paragraphs[0].12] The Disclosure Requirements in ESRS 2, in topical ESRS and in sector-specific ESRS are structured into the following reporting areas: (a) Governance (GOV): the governance processes, controls and procedures used to monitor, manage and oversee impacts, risks and opportunities (see ESRS 2, chapter 2 Governance); (b) Strategy (SBM): how the undertaking’s strategy and business model interact with its material impacts, risks and opportunities, including how the undertaking addresses those impacts, risks and opportunities (see ESRS 2, chapter 3 Strategy); (c) Impact, risk and opportunity management (IRO): the process(es) by which the undertaking: i. identifies impacts, risks and opportunities and assesses their materiality (see IRO-1 in section 4.1 of ESRS 2), ii. manages material sustainability matters through policies and actions (see sec
